newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says Hebron deal hours away, pullout next week.
newsitem.headline: PLO says Hebron deal hours away, pullout next week.

text.p: Palestinian officials said on Monday that Israel and the PLO would reach a Hebron deal within hours and Israeli troops would withdraw from most of the West Bank town within a week.

"Redeployment from Hebron will take place a week after the announcement of an agreement," said negotiator Mohammad Dahlan, head of Palestinian preventive security in the Gaza Strip. An Israeli spokesman declined to comment.
U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross, who pushed and pulled the sides together on orders from President Bill Clinton, was due back from Washington on Monday to mediate any last-minute snags.
Dahlan spoke to Reuters by phone from the self-ruled strip while Palestinian and Israeli negotiators met in Jerusalem to hammer out final details.
"We expect to conclude negotiations on Hebron today. We expect an agreement," chief Palestinian security negotiator Abdel Razak al-Yihye told reporters on his way into the talks.
Dahlan said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were preparing to meet on Tuesday to seal the long-overdue agreement.
Ross would meet Netanyahu at 1630 GMT in Jerusalem, an Israeli spokesman said, and was expected to travel to Gaza for talks with Arafat later on Monday.

Hebron, long a flashpoint of violence between Arabs and Jews, is the last of seven occupied West Bank cities Israel agreed to give self-rule to under an agreement signed with the PLO in 1995. The PLO took over much of the Gaza Strip in 1994.
Chief Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said American and Egyptian officials would attend the Arafat-Netanyahu summit.
"If we manage to reach a compromise over remaining unresolved issues, I believe a summit meeting will be held tomorrow with American and Egyptian participation," he said.

Underscoring tensions in Hebron, Israeli troops arrested several Palestinian construction workers on Monday after Jewish settlers complained they were doing work close to a Jewish enclave in the town, Palestinian witnesses said.
Security concerns have held up the handover, including demands by Netanyahu for measures he says are needed to protect the 400 Jews in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.
Under the 1995 accord, Hebron was due to have been given self-rule nine months ago.

Erekat said the two sides would discuss adding international observers from Turkey, Italy, Sweden and Switzerland to the Norwegian force making up the 200-strong Temporary International Presence in Hebron (TIPH).
In parliament, Israeli legislators debated a motion of no confidence in the government proposed by the right-wing Moledet party opposed to the Hebron deal.

"Netanyahu's government is striding quickly towards a Palestinian state," Moledet leader Rehavam Zeevi said in an address to parliament. The government was expected to easily defeat the no-confidence motion in a vote later on Monday.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai met Arafat on Sunday and later told reporters the two sides were aiming to remove all obstacles to the deal by late on Monday.
